## Introduction

This vignette demonstrates how to turn comma separated categories into tidy rows using `tidyr::separate_longer_delim()`, then summarize and visualize the results with `dplyr` and `ggplot2`. 
The example uses the [Netflix Movies and TV Shows dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/shivamb/netflix-shows) from Kaggle.

## 1. Load packages and import data

Note: Install `tidyverse` if necessary: `install.packages("tidyverse")`.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
netflix <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zxinah/DATA-607-Data-Acquisition-Management-/refs/heads/main/netflix_titles.csv"
)

glimpse(netflix)

# Keep the fields relevant 
netflix_small <- netflix %>%
  select(show_id, title, type, release_year, listed_in)

glimpse(netflix_small)
```

## 2. Column Tidying

The `listed_in` column may contain multiple categories separated by commas. Each row represents a title, but the category field contains several values. To count categories individually, there should be one title category pair per row.

```{r}
netflix_small %>%
  select(title, listed_in) %>%
  slice_head(n = 6)
```

## 3. Separate categories into rows

`separate_longer_delim()` splits a character field on a specified delimiter and duplicates the other columns as needed. `str_trim()` removes spaces surrounding category names. `filter()` removes empty or missing values.

```{r}
netflix_tidy <- netflix_small %>%
  filter(!is.na(listed_in), listed_in != "") %>%
  separate_longer_delim(listed_in, delim = ",") %>%
  mutate(genre = str_trim(listed_in)) %>%
  filter(genre != "") %>%
  select(-listed_in)

netflix_tidy %>%
  select(title, type, genre) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

**Interpretation:** A single title can now appear in multiple rows, once for each category. These are category assignments, not duplicate titles.

## 4. Count and sort categories

`count()` groups by the specified variable and counts rows; `arrange()` sorts results. Because each title can have several categories, the category totals should not be added together to estimate the number of unique titles.

```{r}
genre_counts <- netflix_tidy %>%
  count(genre, name = "titles") %>%
  arrange(desc(titles))

genre_counts %>% slice_head(n = 10)
```

## 5. Compare movies and TV shows

`filter()` can isolate one type of content. Here, `count()` also demonstrates how to group by two variables simultaneously.

```{r}
movie_genres <- netflix_tidy %>%
  filter(type == "Movie") %>%
  count(genre, sort = TRUE, name = "movie_titles")

movie_genres %>% slice_head(n = 8)

by_type <- netflix_tidy %>%
  count(type, genre, name = "titles") %>%
  arrange(type, desc(titles))

by_type %>% slice_head(n = 10)
```

## 6. Visualize the ten most common categories

`ggplot2` turns the summary table into a horizontal bar chart. `reorder()` arranges the category labels by their counts.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5

genre_counts %>%
  slice_max(order_by = titles, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(genre, titles), y = titles)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#C62798") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Ten Most Common Netflix Content Categories",
    x = "Category",
    y = "Number of titles"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

## Conclusion

This demonstrates how `separate_longer_delim()` converts a multi-value column into a tidy, analysis-ready structure. `mutate()` and `str_trim()` clean the resulting text, while `filter()`, `count()`, and `arrange()` support comparisons across content categories. Finally, `ggplot2` visualizes the category frequencies. This workflow can also be applied to survey answers, product tags, and other comma separated fields.

**Data source:** [Netflix Movies and TV Shows on Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/shivamb/netflix-shows).
